d.title: One parameter, a string, always - and why that is the point
d.caption: **The declaration the model sees has exactly one field, and that constraint is the most useful thing the base class does for you.** The model's job shrinks to writing a good query rather than guessing at filters, page sizes and result counts it has no basis for choosing — and every retrieval tool in the system then presents the same interface. **Which leaves the description doing the routing:** with three corpora, the descriptions are the only thing telling them apart, so write each one as an index rather than a label.

d.title: A miss returns a sentence - and the sentence is where hallucination starts
d.caption: **Returning “no matching document found” rather than raising is what lets the turn continue**, so the agent can apologise, ask a clarifying question or search again. But a model handed that sentence and *no instruction about what to do with it* will frequently answer from its own weights, fluently and without hedging. **That is the most common RAG failure in production and it is invisible in testing**, because the answer looks exactly like a good one — which is why the rule has to be in the instruction and then actually evaluated.

d.title: A document id in the text is the cheapest citation there is
d.caption: **The `[refund-policy]` prefix is not decoration.** Return the id with each chunk, instruct the model to name what it used, and the answer arrives attributable — which is what makes a wrong answer diagnosable rather than merely wrong. **For the provider's own grounded tools you get structured grounding metadata instead**, which is richer and arrives without asking; for your own corpus, an id in the retrieved string is enough to start and costs nothing.

d.title: Four patterns, and the round trip each one adds
d.caption: **Read the right-hand column before the left, because the instinct to add all four is strong.** A naive RAG turn is two model calls; rewrite and retry makes three; validation and reflection take you to five or six, each carrying the conversation. **That is the right trade for a medical or legal answer and the wrong one for a product FAQ** where a miss costs nothing — and the agent you end up with takes nine seconds to answer a question about opening hours.

d.title: Retrieve, judge, retry - and the cap that stops the bill
d.caption: **Three things make this better than instructing the model to try harder.** The retry is bounded, so a corpus that will never answer costs three searches rather than an open-ended argument. The judgement is structured, so your code branches on `sufficient` instead of parsing prose. And the rewritten query is explicit, **so you can log it and discover what your users ask versus what your documents say** — which is often the most valuable artefact of the whole pattern. If three well-chosen queries miss, the fourth almost never saves you.

d.title: Reflection checks every answer; evaluation tells you whether to
d.caption: **A reflection step checks every answer at runtime, for every user, forever; an evaluation suite checks a sample offline, once per change.** Build the evaluation first — it is cheaper, repeatable, and frequently shows groundedness already at 97%, which means the runtime check would pay a full round trip to catch three cases in a hundred. **Add reflection when the cost of those three is high:** regulated advice, medical information, anything with a legal consequence.
